params.question: Clinical findings such as a uterus larger than expected for dates and auscultation of two separate fetal heartbeats are sufficient to confirm a diagnosis of twin pregnancy.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually false. The video explained that clinical signs like a uterus larger than dates, severe vomiting, and hearing two heartbeats can suggest twins but are not reliable on their own. Ultrasound is the only definitive way to diagnose a multiple pregnancy, and the first-trimester scan (11–14 weeks) is essential for determining chorionicity — the single most important prognostic factor.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. While these clinical signs raise suspicion, they are not reliable enough to confirm a multiple pregnancy on their own. Ultrasound is the definitive diagnostic tool and should be performed routinely at the first-trimester scan (11–14 weeks) to confirm the number of fetuses and determine chorionicity.

params.question: On first-trimester ultrasound of a twin pregnancy, a wedge of placental tissue is seen projecting into the base of the inter-twin membrane, creating a peak. What does this lambda sign indicate?

answers.text: Monochorionic diamniotic twins sharing a single placenta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In monochorionic twins, the membrane is composed only of amnion and meets the placenta at a sharp right angle, producing a T-sign — not a wedge of placental tissue.

Correct. The lambda (twin peak) sign occurs because chorionic villi from both placentas grow into the base of the inter-twin membrane, creating a visible wedge. This confirms dichorionic placentation — the lowest-risk twin configuration.

answers.text: Monochorionic monoamniotic twins with no inter-twin membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In monoamniotic twins, there is no inter-twin membrane at all — the babies share a single amniotic sac. The lambda sign requires a visible membrane with placental tissue at its base.

answers.text: A vanishing twin with residual placental tissue at the membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A vanishing twin refers to one twin that stops developing and is reabsorbed early in pregnancy. The lambda sign is a normal finding in dichorionic twins — the wedge results from villi of both placentas growing into the membrane base, not from reabsorbing tissue.

overallFeedback.feedback: The lambda (twin peak) sign indicates dichorionic diamniotic twins. Villi from both separate placentas grow into the membrane base, creating the characteristic wedge. Contrast this with the T-sign of monochorionic twins, where only amniotic membrane meets the placenta at a right angle.

The lambda sign is pathognomonic of dichorionic diamniotic twins. Remember that this sign is most reliably seen before 14 weeks — after that, membrane thickening reduces chorionicity determination accuracy significantly.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman with monochorionic diamniotic twins diagnosed at her 12-week

params.question: A 30-year-old woman with monochorionic diamniotic twins diagnosed at her 12-week scan presents for antenatal care planning. Which surveillance schedule and planned delivery timing is appropriate?

answers.text: Growth scans every 4 weeks from 20 weeks; planned delivery at 38 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the protocol for dichorionic diamniotic (DCDA) twins, which have separate placentas and lower risk. MCDA twins share one placenta and need more frequent monitoring to detect twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome early.

answers.text: Ultrasound scans every 2 weeks from 16 weeks; planned delivery at 36 to 37 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. MCDA twins share one placenta, so twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome can develop within days. Fortnightly scans from 16 weeks allow early detection, and delivery is planned at 36–37 weeks before placental ageing causes complications.

answers.text: Inpatient monitoring from 28 weeks; planned caesarean delivery at 32 to 34 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This intensive protocol is reserved for monochorionic monoamniotic (MCMA) twins, who share a single amniotic sac and face cord entanglement risk. MCDA twins have a membrane separating them and do not require inpatient monitoring.

answers.text: Monthly scans from 24 weeks with Doppler; planned delivery at 40 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No multiple pregnancy should be allowed to continue to 40 weeks. Even DCDA twins — the lowest-risk category — are delivered at 38 weeks. MCDA twins need fortnightly surveillance from 16 weeks with delivery at 36–37 weeks.

overallFeedback.feedback: For MCDA twins, the correct protocol is fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks with planned delivery at 36–37 weeks. Remember the principle: chorionicity determines the entire surveillance schedule — more shared structures mean higher risk and more intensive monitoring.

Surveillance intensity tracks directly with shared placental and amniotic risk: DCDA (4-weekly, 38 weeks) → MCDA (fortnightly from 16 weeks, 36–37 weeks) → MCMA (inpatient from 28 weeks, 32–34 weeks by caesarean).
